entry: Partially recognized state in the Horn of Africa, on the southern coast of the [[Gulf of Aden]]. Its claimed territory covers 176,120 sq km (68,000 sq mi), with approximately 6.2 million people as of 2024; the capital and largest city is Hargeisa. In the late 19th century the [[United Kingdom]] established the Somaliland Protectorate. The State of Somaliland gained independence from the United Kingdom on June 26, 1960, and five days later united with the former Italian Somalia to form the Somali Republic. After the union proved problematic, Somaliland declared independence again in 1991, and its governments since then have been democratically elected and have sought international recognition. [[Israel]] became the first and only UN member state to formally recognize it, on December 26, 2025. Somalia does not recognize its independence and regards the area as one of its federal member states.

Subset of the [[Sensory nervous system|sensory nervous system]] that detects touch, temperature, pain and body position. Its main functions are perceiving external and internal stimuli and regulating body position and balance (proprioception). It has been thought of as having two subdivisions: one for mechanosensory information, such as light touch, vibration, pressure and tension in the [[Skin]], and one for nociception, the detection of pain and temperature deemed harmful. Mechanoreceptors such as tactile corpuscles, which respond to pressure and vibration, are among the cutaneous receptors. Signals travel to the [[Spinal cord]], where they may drive a [[Reflex|reflex]], and to the brain for conscious perception. Neighboring neurons in the somatosensory cortex represent nearby areas of skin, forming a sensory homunculus. As of 2024, debate continued over the underlying mechanisms of the model.

Ceremonial county (pop., 2024: 1,012,934) in South West England, bordered by [[Bristol]] and Gloucestershire to the north and [[Devon]] to the southwest. Largely rural, it is dominated in the center by the Levels, a coastal [[Wetland|wetland]] plain. The county played a significant part in the rise to power of [[Alfred the Great]] and in the English Civil War. The largest settlement, the city of Bath, famous for Georgian architecture, is a UNESCO [[World Heritage Site]]. The county is also home to the Glastonbury Festival, one of the UK's major music festivals.

Method of using sound propagation, usually underwater, to navigate, measure distances and detect objects. It stands for sound navigation and ranging. Passive sonar listens for sounds made by vessels, while active sonar emits pulses of sound and listens for their [[Reflection (physics)|echoes]]. Sonar is also used for robot navigation and, in its upward-looking in-air form called sodar, for atmospheric research. The first recorded use, attributed to [[Leonardo da Vinci]] in 1490, involved a tube inserted into water to detect vessels by ear. Sonar was developed during [[World War I]] to counter the threat of [[Submarine|submarine]] warfare, and an operational passive system was in use by 1918.

Multi-movement instrumental composition, usually of three or four movements, which may be written for various instruments. By the early 19th century the sonata represented a principle of composing large-scale works, and it was regarded, with the [[Fugue]], as one of two fundamental methods of organizing concert music. After the Baroque period most sonatas were written for a solo instrument, most often a keyboard instrument, or for a solo instrument with keyboard accompaniment. Arcangelo Corelli's twelve chamber trio sonatas of Op. 2 (1685) were foundational to the form. A short or technically easy sonata is called a sonatina. Notable examples include [[Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart|Mozart]]'s Piano Sonata No. 11 in A major, K. 331, and [[Ludwig van Beethoven|Beethoven]]'s Piano Sonata No. 14 in C-sharp minor, Op. 27 No. 2, known as the "Moonlight".

Genus of flowering plants in the daisy family ([[Asteraceae]]), commonly known as sow thistles. They are annual, biennial or perennial herbs, and a few are woody, restricted to the [[Canary Islands]] and [[Madeira]]. The plants exude a milky latex when cut, and the common name comes from the belief that feeding them to lactating sows would increase milk production. Native to [[Eurasia]] and tropical Africa, they are now found almost worldwide in temperate regions, where in many areas they are considered noxious weeds. *Sonchus arvensis*, the perennial sow thistle, is regarded as the most economically detrimental. Young leaves are edible, and the plants are common hosts for [[Aphid|aphids]]. Plants of the World Online accepted 106 species as of March 2023.

Musical composition performed by the [[Human voice|human voice]], which usually carries a [[Melody|melody]] in sections that are often repeated or varied. A song without instruments is called a cappella. Words written for music are called lyrics. A pre-existing poem set to composed music in the classical tradition is an art song, while simple songs learned informally by ear are called folk songs, and songs designed for the mass market are called popular songs. Larger classical vocal forms such as [[Opera|opera]] and oratorio use terms such as [[Aria|aria]] instead. The word can also refer to instrumental pieces, such as the 19th-century *Songs Without Words* for solo piano.

Imperial dynasty of China, 960–1279. It was founded by Emperor Taizu of Song, who usurped the Later Zhou throne and conquered the rest of the Ten Kingdoms, ending the [[Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period]]. The Northern Song (960–1127) had its capital at Bianjing (now Kaifeng) and controlled most of East China. After losing the north to the Jurchen-led [[Jin dynasty (1115–1234)|Jin dynasty]], the Southern Song (1127–1279) moved its capital to Lin'an (now [[Hangzhou]]). [[Kublai Khan]] founded the [[Yuan dynasty]] in 1271 and conquered the Song in 1279 at the Battle of Yamen. The Song was the first in world history to issue banknotes or true paper money and the first Chinese government to maintain a permanent standing navy. China's population doubled between the 10th and 11th centuries, and the Northern Song is estimated to have had 90 million people. The philosopher [[Zhu Xi]] helped reinvigorate [[Confucianism]] as Neo-Confucianism.

Epic poem in Old French, the oldest surviving major work of [[French literature]] and the first example of the chanson de geste. It recounts the deeds of the Frankish military leader Roland at the Battle of Roncevaux Pass in AD 778, during the reign of [[Charlemagne]]. The poem was written centuries after the events, probably between about 1040 and 1115, and possibly by a poet named Turold. Those favoring an earlier date argue that it influenced the [[First Crusade]] (1096–1099). Its single surviving manuscript, dated between 1129 and 1165 and written in Anglo-Norman, is held by the Bodleian Library at the [[University of Oxford]]. After two manuscripts were found in 1832 and 1835 and published in 1837, the poem became recognized as France's national epic.

Bird of the suborder Passeri, one of the two major lineages of [[Bird|perching birds]], with about 4,000 species. The other lineage, the Tyranni, has about 1,000 species. Recent estimates place the origin of songbirds about 50 million years ago, in Australia, and about 40 million years ago they began spreading to Eurasia, Africa and eventually the Americas. Songs are essentially territorial and also signal sexual intentions, made possible by the syrinx, a bony vocal organ where the windpipe meets the bronchial tubes. Vocal mimicry is almost entirely restricted to songbirds, and some, such as the [[Lyrebird|lyrebirds]] and [[Mockingbird|mockingbirds]], excel at imitating other birds and environmental noises. Many members of the crow family ([[Corvidae]]) communicate with croaks or screeches.

West African state in the western [[Sahel]] during the 15th and 16th centuries, one of the largest African empires in history. Under Sonni Ali, who made Gao its capital, the Songhai expanded by absorbing vast regions of the [[Mali Empire]]. [[Timbuktu]] and Djenné were conquered in 1468 and 1475, respectively. The Sonni dynasty (c. 1464–1493) was succeeded by the Askia dynasty (1493–1591). Muhammad Ture, known as [[Askia Muhammad I|Askia the Great]], overthrew Sonni Ali's son and instituted political and economic reforms. Later plots, coups and civil wars caused decline. In 1590 Al-Mansur of Morocco sent an army under Judar Pasha to seize control of the [[Trans-Saharan trade]] routes, and the empire collapsed after its defeat at the Battle of Tondibi in 1591.

entry: Double album by [[Stevie Wonder]], released on September 28, 1976, by Tamla Records. It is regarded as the culmination of Wonder's classic period, and it debuted at number one on the Billboard 200, the third album to do so and the first by an American artist. Its lead single "I Wish" and follow-up "Sir Duke" both reached number one on the Billboard Hot 100. It won Album of the Year at the 19th [[Grammy Awards]] and was certified Diamond by the RIAA in 2005. The [[Library of Congress]] added it to the National Recording Registry in 2005.

Italian-born Indian politician and longest-serving president of the [[Indian National Congress]]. She married [[Rajiv Gandhi]] in 1968, after meeting him in Cambridge, England, and moved to India. She entered politics in 1997 and was Congress president from 1998 to 2017 and again from 2019 to 2022. After the 2004 elections she declined the premiership and led the United Progressive Alliance coalition instead. Her foreign birth was a subject of public debate, and since 2024 she has represented Rajasthan in the Rajya Sabha.

Sound produced by shock waves from an object traveling faster than the [[Speed of sound|speed of sound]]. A sonic boom sounds similar to an explosion or a [[Thunder|thunderclap]], and the crack of a supersonic bullet is a small example. [[Mach number|Mach 1]] is about 1,192 km/h (741 mph) at sea level and 20 °C (68 °F). The boom is a continuous effect, heard only by observers whom the cone-shaped region trailing the object passes over. Large supersonic aircraft can startle people and cause minor damage, leading to prohibitions on routine overland supersonic flight.

Video game and media franchise created by [[Sega]], centered on a supersonic blue hedgehog who battles the scientist Doctor Eggman. The first game, released in 1991 for the [[Sega Genesis]], was developed to give Sega a mascot to rival Nintendo's [[Mario]]. The main games are platformers mostly developed by Sonic Team, with spin-offs in racing, fighting, party and sports genres. The franchise also includes printed media, animations, films and merchandise. Series sales and free-to-play mobile downloads totaled 1.77 billion as of 2024. The franchise's fandom produces unofficial works such as fan art and fan games.

Norwegian figure skater and film star. Henie won three Olympic gold medals in women's singles, in 1928, 1932 and 1936, and was a ten-time world champion from 1927 to 1936. She also won six consecutive European titles from 1931 to 1936. She was one of only two skaters to defend a women's singles Olympic title, the other being Katarina Witt. At the height of her American acting career she was one of the highest-paid stars in Hollywood, appearing in box-office hits such as *Thin Ice* (1937) and *Sun Valley Serenade* (1941). Her shorter skating attire and ballet-influenced routines transformed the presentation of [[Figure skating]].

Fixed poetic form of fourteen lines, traditionally with a set rhyme scheme, originating in 13th-century [[Sicily]]. The word derives from the Italian *sonetto*, meaning "little song". Giacomo da Lentini is credited with inventing the form at the court of Frederick II in [[Palermo]]. It spread to many European-language areas, mainly to express romantic love at first, and Guittone d'Arezzo later brought it to [[Tuscany]]. The Italian sonnet developed an octave that states a problem and a sestet that offers a resolution, with a turn, or *volta*, usually at the ninth line. [[Petrarch]], the most influential Italian sonneteer, typically used an ABBAABBA octave, which became the standard pattern. Modern variations have abandoned the fourteen-line limit and even rhyme.

Japanese multinational conglomerate headquartered in Minato, [[Tokyo]]. Founded in 1946 as Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo, the company took the name Sony Corporation in 1958 and became known for products such as the TR-55 transistor radio and the Walkman. It acquired CBS Records in 1988 and [[Columbia Pictures]] in 1989. In 1994 it entered the console market with the [[PlayStation (console)|PlayStation]], which has sold over 650 million units. Since 2021 it has operated Crunchyroll, the world's largest anime streaming platform. In 2021 it was renamed Sony Group Corporation as a holding company.

American film and television company owned by Japan's [[Sony]]. Founded on December 18, 1987, as Columbia Pictures Entertainment, it was formed from a spinoff of [[The Coca-Cola Company|Coca-Cola]]'s entertainment business and a merger with Tri-Star Pictures. Sony acquired the studio in 1989 and renamed it Sony Pictures Entertainment in 1991. Based at the Sony Pictures Studios lot in Culver City, California, it is one of the major American film studios known as the Big Four. It produces, acquires and distributes motion pictures and television programs.

Chinese politician and activist, the wife of [[Sun Yat-sen]] and known as the "Mother of Modern China". Born in Shanghai and educated in the United States, she married Sun as his third wife in 1915. She became a strong advocate of the alliance between the [[Kuomintang]] and the [[Chinese Communist Party]], opposing [[Chiang Kai-shek]]'s split with the Communists in 1927. During the [[Second Sino-Japanese War]] she joined her sisters in wartime [[Chongqing]] to support national unity. She backed the Communists in the Chinese Civil War and held senior posts after the People's Republic of China was proclaimed in 1949. Her Beijing home was invaded by Red Guards during the [[Cultural Revolution]], though she was protected from purges. In May 1981, during her final illness, she was named Honorary Chairman of the People's Republic of China.

Mass of impure carbon particles produced by the incomplete [[Combustion|combustion]] of [[Hydrocarbon|hydrocarbons]]. Considered a hazardous, [[Carcinogen|carcinogenic]] substance, soot causes various types of [[Cancer]] and lung disease. The term broadly covers all particulate matter from the process, including residues of [[Coal]] and petroleum coke, and sometimes polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and heavy metals such as mercury. Carbon black, a nearly pure form of carbon made intentionally, is not found in regular soot. Black carbon, a term used in atmospheric science, describes light-absorbing particles that are second only to CO₂ itself as a contributor to short-term global warming.

Italian actress and one of the last surviving major stars of the Golden Age of Hollywood. Encouraged to take acting lessons after entering a beauty pageant, she began her film career in 1950. A five-picture contract with Paramount in 1956 launched her international career, and during the 1950s she was one of the best-known sex symbols of her time. Her performance in *Two Women* (1960), directed by [[Vittorio De Sica]], won her the Academy Award for Best Actress, the first Oscar for a non-English-language performance. She holds the record for seven David di Donatello Awards for Best Actress and has received an Academy Honorary Award. She appeared opposite [[Cary Grant]] in *Houseboat* and opposite [[Marcello Mastroianni]] in *Marriage Italian Style*.

Professional itinerant teacher in [[Ancient Greece]] during the fifth and fourth centuries BC. Sophists taught subjects such as [[Philosophy|philosophy]], [[Rhetoric|rhetoric]], music, athletics and mathematics, and sold their tutoring mainly to young statesmen and nobility. The first credited sophist, Protagoras, argued that "man is the measure of all things" and openly strove to "make the weaker argument the stronger". Critics among the philosophers of [[Classical Athens]], notably [[Plato]] and [[Aristotle]], faulted sophists for valuing clever speech over the pursuit of truth, and their name later became a term of disparagement. Today a sophist is a person who reasons with clever but deceptive or intellectually dishonest arguments.

Ancient Greek [[Tragedy|tragedian]], one of three principal dramatists of classical Greek tragedy, alongside [[Aeschylus]] and [[Euripides]]. He wrote more than 120 plays, of which seven survive complete, among them *Ajax*, *Antigone*, *Oedipus Rex*, *Electra* and *Oedipus at Colonus*. For almost 50 years he was the most celebrated playwright in the dramatic competitions of [[Athens]], winning 24 of the 30 he entered and never placing lower than second. [[Aristotle]] credits him with adding a third [[Actor|actor]], reducing the importance of the chorus and developing his characters more fully than earlier playwrights. In 441 BC he was elected one of Athens's ten generals, serving as a junior colleague of [[Pericles]].

Public research university in [[Paris]], France, formed in 2018 by the merger of Paris-Sorbonne University (Paris IV) and Pierre and Marie Curie University (Paris VI). Its legacy reaches back to 1257, when Robert de Sorbon founded the College of Sorbonne as a constituent college of the University of Paris. [[Marie Curie|Marie Skłodowska-Curie]], who came from Poland in 1891, was the first woman to become a professor there, and she and her husband [[Pierre Curie]] are considered founders of the modern Faculty of Science and Engineering. The university claims that its alumni and professors have won 33 [[Nobel Prize|Nobel Prizes]], six [[Fields Medal|Fields Medals]] and one Turing Award, as of 2021.
